title: Compound interest: money that grows on itself
summary: See why savings grow faster every year when interest earns interest, and why time matters more than the amount.
objective: Work out a compound balance year by year and explain why starting early beats starting big.

hook.prompt: Which would you rather have in 30 years?

options.text: $1,000 put away today, growing at 10% a year with interest added to the balance

options.feedback: It looks like more, but $1,000 growing at 10% a year becomes about $17,449, not $4,000.

options.text: They come out about the same
options.feedback: Adding $100 a year would give $4,000. Because the interest itself earns interest, it reaches about $17,449.

hook.explanation: $1,000 at 10% a year grows to about $17,449 in 30 years, because each year's interest earns interest too.

bricks.title: Interest on interest
bricks.body: **Interest** is the price of money: a bank pays it on your savings, and a lender charges it on a loan. At 10% a year, $100 earns $10. With **compound interest**, that $10 joins the balance, so next year you earn 10% of $110: $11. **Simple interest** would pay only on the first $100, so $10 every year.

term.definition: Interest paid on the balance, including the interest already added, so each year's interest is bigger.

visual.alt: A table of $100 at 10% compound interest: $110 after year 1, $121 after year 2, and $133.10 after year 3.

bricks.prompt: You save $200 at 10% a year, compounded yearly. How much do you have after 2 years?

options.feedback: That's simple interest: $20 twice. In year 2 the interest is 10% of $220, so it's $22.
That's after 1 year. Add a second year's interest, worked out on $220.
That would be 100% growth. 10% of $200 is only $20 in the first year.

bricks.hint: Work out year 1, then use that new balance for year 2.
bricks.explanation:
Year 2 earns interest on $220, not $200.
Year 1: $200 + $20 = $220
Year 2: $220 + $22 = $242

bricks.prompt: Both accounts start with $1,000 at 5% a year. Which one pays compound interest?

visual.alt: Account A: interest of $50, $50, and $50, with balances of $1,050, $1,100, and $1,150.

options.feedback: Account A earns the same $50 every year, paid on the first $1,000 only. That's simple interest.

visual.alt: Account B: interest of $50, $52.50, and $55.13, with balances of $1,050, $1,102.50, and $1,157.63.

bricks.hint: Look at the interest column. Does it stay the same or grow?
bricks.explanation: Account B's interest grows each year, because 5% is taken of a balance that already includes past interest.

bricks.title: The shortcut: multiply by 1 + the rate
bricks.body: So far you added each year's interest by hand. A quicker way: multiply the balance by **1 plus the rate**, with the rate as a decimal. At 10%, that's × 1.1: $100 × 1.1 = $110, then $110 × 1.1 = $121. The 1 keeps what you had; the 0.1 adds the interest. For several years, multiply once per year, which is what the power \( n \) means below.

term.definition: The amount you start with, written \( P \). The rate is \( r \) and the number of years is \( n \).

bricks.prompt: Complete the rule for a balance that grows 8% a year.
bricks.template: Each year, multiply the balance by [[g]].

mistakes.feedback: 0.08 gives only the interest and drops the balance itself. Add the 1 to keep what you had.
1.8 would be 80% growth. 8% as a decimal is 0.08, so the factor is 1.08.

bricks.hint: Write 8% as a decimal, then add the 1 that keeps the balance.
bricks.explanation: 8% is 0.08, and 1 + 0.08 = 1.08: the whole balance plus 8% more.

bricks.prompt: Which calculation gives the balance of $1,000 left at 10% a year for 3 years?

options.feedback: That adds 10% three times to the first $1,000 only, which is simple interest. Each year should grow the new balance.
Multiplying by 3 triples the money. Multiply by 1.1 once for each year instead.
0.1 alone is just the interest, and cubing it makes it tiny. Use 1.1 so the balance is kept.

bricks.hint: Multiply by 1 + the rate once for every year.
bricks.explanation:
Each year multiplies the balance by 1.1, three times over.
$1,000 × 1.1 × 1.1 × 1.1 = $1,331

bricks.title: Time does most of the work
bricks.body: Now stretch the years out. $1,000 at 10% gains about $1,594 in its first 10 years, but about $10,722 in its third decade, from $6,727 to $17,449. The rate never changes; the balance it's taken of keeps getting bigger. So compounding looks slow at first and fast later, and the years at the end only pay off if the money went in early.

bricks.prompt: Why does the third decade add so much more than the first, at the same 10% rate?

options.text: 10% of a bigger balance is a bigger amount
The rate rises the longer you save
options.feedback: The rate stays at 10% the whole time. What changes is the balance it's taken of.

options.text: You add more money in later years
options.feedback: Nothing is added after the first $1,000. All the growth comes from interest.

bricks.hint: What stays the same over the 30 years, and what keeps growing?
bricks.explanation: In year 1, 10% is taken of $1,000. In year 30 it's taken of over $15,000, so the same rate brings in far more.

bricks.prompt: Sam puts $1,000 away at 10% a year at age 25. Priya puts $2,000 away at 10% a year at age 35. Neither adds more. Who has more at 65?

options.feedback: Priya starts with twice as much, but by age 35 Sam's $1,000 has already grown to about $2,594, and it keeps that lead.
They'd be equal only if Sam's money exactly doubled in his first 10 years. At 10% it grows to about $2,594, more than Priya's $2,000.

bricks.hint: How much has Sam's $1,000 grown to by the time Priya starts?
bricks.explanation:
Sam's money compounds for 40 years and Priya's for 30.
Sam at 35: about $2,594, ahead of Priya's $2,000
Both then grow at 10%, so Sam stays ahead.

challenge.prompt: You owe $500 on a loan that charges 20% a year, compounded yearly. You pay nothing for 3 years. How much do you owe then?

options.feedback: That's simple interest: $100 a year on the first $500. Each year, 20% is charged on the bigger balance.
That's after 2 years. Multiply by 1.2 once more for the third year.
That multiplies by the number of years. Multiply by 1.2 once for each year instead.

challenge.hint: Compounding works the same on a loan: multiply by 1 + the rate once a year.
challenge.explanation:
Each year adds 20% of the new balance.
Year 1: $500 × 1.2 = $600
Year 2: $600 × 1.2 = $720
Year 3: $720 × 1.2 = $864

takeaways: Compound interest pays interest on past interest, so each year's gain is bigger than the last.
To find a balance, multiply by 1 + the rate once for every year.
Time does most of the work: start saving early, and pay off compounding debts early.
